result.title: AI is already in the theatre of war just not on the side of the patient: clinical chatbots, telemedicine, and an agenda for "AI for medical humanity".
result.authorString: Prigg AR, Robinson H, Alkhalil M, Gough J.

result.abstractText: Artificial intelligence (AI) is already embedded in modern warfare, mainly through surveillance, targeting, and military decision-making. However, its potential to support clinicians and patients in conflict settings remains underdeveloped. Frontline medical teams must make time-critical, high-stakes decisions with scarce diagnostics, disrupted referrals, insecure communications, changing injury patterns, and irregular access to specialist expertise. Humanitarian medicine needs a proactive clinician-facing AI agenda that strengthens clinical judgment, not replaces it. We propose a two-stage model: a bounded, protocol-anchored chatbot as the "first mile" of point-of-care support, and telemedicine as the "second mile" for specialist oversight and accountability. The chatbot would structure assessments, guide protocol-based actions, identify missing information and areas of uncertainty, generate standard handovers, and trigger escalations. Remote specialists would provide context and retain responsibility for clinical decisions. Safe deployment requires transparent protocols, constrained scope, hard refusals, awareness of uncertainty, data minimisation, offline-first functionality, adversarial threat modelling, and safeguards against coercive or dual-use applications. Evaluation should use locally informed simulation, silent deployment, prospective monitoring of deviations and harms, predefined safety thresholds, and independent humanitarian oversight before wider clinical use. AI will increasingly shape conflict medicine, with or without humanitarian engagement. The priority is to ensure design, governance, and evaluation are guided by patient safety, medical neutrality, local involvement, and clinical accountability, placing AI on the side of the patient, not the machinery of war.

result.title: When should mental health chatbots have a duty to report?
result.authorString: Palmieri S, Joralemon V, Cohen IG.
result.abstractText: People increasingly disclose suicidal intent, child abuse and threats of violence to AI chatbots. Made to a clinician, such disclosures would trigger mandated-reporting statutes, Tarasoff -style duties to protect third parties and a duty of care toward patients at risk of self-harm. Made to a chatbot, they trigger almost none. The first chatbot-specific laws, in California and New York, require crisis referrals but impose no duty to report or intervene. We argue that a chatbot’s legal duties should follow the function it holds itself out as serving. We distinguish FDA-regulated mental-health devices, chatbots marketed as therapeutic or emotional support, and general-purpose conversational AI. For the middle category we propose five duties: detection of defined risk indicators, human review before external escalation, proportionate crisis response, independent audit and record-keeping. We then examine enforcement through market-access statutes and litigation, and the confidentiality questions any reporting regime raises.

result.title: LLM-Based Chatbots and the Suicidal Crisis: Relational Hallucination as a Bi-Logical Process
result.authorString: Andrisano Ruggieri R, Ragosta A, Balcombe L.
result.abstractText: A series of documented deaths by suicide following prolonged interactions with chatbots based on large language models (LLMs) has exposed the clinical risks of delegating emotional support to conversational artificial intelligence. This paper proposes a psychodynamic account of these events, integrating the bi-logical theory of Ignacio Matte Blanco, the Freudian theory of primary hallucination, and the analysis of demand elaborated by Carli and Paniccia. The suicidal crisis is conceptualized as a pathological prevalence of symmetric logic, marked by the generalization, maximization, and irradiation of psychic pain and by the collapse of temporality, while LLM-based chatbots are conceptualized as systems of pure formal asymmetry lacking any symmetric, emotional, and embodied base. Their encounter generates what we call relational hallucination: an unconscious, structurally determined process, homologous to primary hallucination, through which the subject in crisis invests the chatbot with relational qualities perceived as real. Because the process obeys the laws of symmetric logic, it cannot be corrected by information alone. The chatbot, responding to the explicit request rather than to the unconscious demand it conveys, produces an amplificatory collusion that reinforces the premises of the crisis. The failure of algorithmic support in acute suicidal states is therefore ontological rather than technical. Implications for clinical training, regulation, and research are discussed.
